Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Naixin Zhang and Tong Lin”
State Key Laboratory of General Artificial Intelligence,
School of Intelligence Science and Technology,
Peking University, Beijing 100871, China

Abstract

Reinforcement learning (RL) for retrieval-
augmented language models enables policies
to interleave generated reasoning with retrieved
observations. However, in Search-R1-style
PPO, training may become unstable after the
model has already reached strong validation
performance. This paper studies late-stage col-
lapse as a training-stability problem in search-
based RL. Four metrics are proposed to quan-
tify validation drawdown (VDD), adyantage-
tail expansion (ATE), actor update stress (AUS),
and observation-to-actor contamination in gen-
eralized advantage estimation (GAE), denoted
as OAGC. The analysis further shows how ob-
servation tokens can influence actor updates
through value targets, value-model learning,
and GAE. To address this issue, Observation-
aware Stabilization (OAS) combines observa-
tion residual decay, old-value anchoring, and
boundary smoothing. On three benchmark
datasets (NQ, TriviaQA, and HotpotQA), OAS
improves Search-R1 PPO under multiple re-
trieval budgets. In the main Top-3 setting, our
method improves the exact match (EM) mea-
sure from 31.8/49.6/18.7 to 37.6/56.8/23.9 and
reduces OAGC from 0.331 to 0.088, with lower
search-budget saturation and no increase in the
no-search rate.

1 Introduction

Large language models are increasingly used as
reasoning agents that interact with external environ-
ments. In knowledge-intensive question answering,
retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) retrieves ex-
ternal evidence before generation (Lewis et al.,
3020), but a single-pass pipeline is often insuffi-
cient for multi-hop evidence gathering, query refor-
mulation, and intermediate verification (Gao et al.,
2023). Recent work on agentic RAG and tool-use
RL therefore invokes search tools during reasoning,
including ReAct (Yao et al., 2023) and Search-R1
(Jin et al., 2025). These methods model question

answering as a multi-step trajectory that interleaves
reasoning, actions, and observations (Xiong et al.,
2025; Qian et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025).

This paradigm makes reinforcement learning a
natural framework for optimizing search-tool be-
havior from outcome-level rewards or process-level
feedback, unlike supervised fine-tuning on fixed
human-annotated or distilled trajectories. RL can
teach models when to search, how to reformulate
queries, how to use retrieved evidence, and when to
stop Gin et al., 2025). In Search-R 1 -style training,
the search engine is incorporated into the environ-
ment, and interactive search-reasoning trajectories
can be optimized with PPO (Schulman et al., 2017;
Jin et al., 2025) or GRPO (Shao et al., 2024; Jin
et al., 2025).

However, interactive search reasoning can also
introduce severe stability problems. Prior work on
multi-turn agent RL and LLM RL has reported re-
ward collapse, entropy collapse, policy staleness,
and gradient spikes in long-sequence OF multi-turn
environments (Wang et al., 2025; Zheng et al.,
2025; Dong et al., 2026a). These findings sug-
gest that search-tool RL should be evaluated not
only by final answer accuracy but also by whether
mode} behavior and optimization signals remain
stable during training.

Our reproduction experiments show that this sta-
bility cannot be guaranteed. We observe a late-
stage failure mode distinct from failing to learn:
the model reaches a reasonable intermediate valida-
tion score, but later suffers a validation drawdown
while both tool use and answer generation degrade.
Final scores cannot distinguish such late-stage col-
lapse from consistently low-scoring runs.

We analyze this late-stage collapse problem
through the token structure of search trajectories.
A single sequence contains both generated tokens
and observation tokens. Generated tokens are ac-
tions sampled by the actor. In contrast, observa-
tion tokens are environmental feedback returned

by the retriever. Although they remain in the con-
text, observation tokens should not directly con-
tribute to the actor loss because they are external
feedback rather than actions sampled by the policy.
Throughout the paper, observation tokens denote
retriever-returned text, observation residuals denote
their temporal-difference (TD) residual terms, and
generated-token advantages denote advantages at
actor-loss positions. Existing implementations typ-
ically mask observation tokens out of the actor loss
(Jin et al., 2025; Chai et al., 2025), but they rarely
explain their role in value fitting, TD residuals,
generalized advantage estimation (GABE), and ad-
vantage propagation (Schulman et al., 2016, 2017).
This paper therefore asks whether the current treat-
ment can transmit observation-side value errors
or TD residuals into generated-token advantages,
thereby affecting late-stage stability.

We therefore examine training stability through
token-level signals rather than final scores alone.
Our analysis first defines late-stage collapse as a
validation drawdown after an earlier performance
peak. It then asks whether this collapse is accom-
panied by systematic gaps between generated and
observation tokens in actor-critic signals. We fur-
ther ask whether these signals can guide a stabiliza-
tion method that preserves observations as context
while reducing their interference with generated-
token policy updates.

To answer these questions, we use four diag-
nostic metrics for training dynamics: validation
drawdown (VDD), advantage tail expansion (ATE),
actor update stress (AUS), and observation-to-actor
GAE contamination (OAGC). These metrics sum-
marize performance drawdown, advantage-tail ex-
Pansion, actor update pressure, and observation-to-
actor contamination. Guided by these diagnostics,
we trace how observation-side residuals can affect
generated-token advantages through value-target
construction, value-model updates, and GAE. This
motivates Observation-aware Stabilization (OAS),
which down-weights observation-side TD residu-
als, anchors value drift around observation spans,
and smooths abrupt boundary value changes while
keeping observation tokens available as context,

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

1. We introduce a diagnostic suite of VDD, ATE,
AUS, and OAGC. These metrics character-
ize late-stage collapse from four perspectives:
performance drawdown, advantage tails, ac-
tor update pressure, and observation-to-actor

GAE contamination.

2. We conduct a token-level mechanism analysis
that Separates value, return, and advantage
signals for generated and observation tokens.
We use OAGC and domain gaps to trace how

observation-side errors enter generated-token
advantages.

3. We propose Observation-aware Stabilization
(OAS), which Stabilizes search-tool PPO
through observation residual decay, old-value
anchoring, and boundary smoothing. Main
results and ablations show that OAS improves
€xact match and reduces nVDD, ATE, and
OAGC. The time-aligned analysis further con-
nects ATE, AUS, and OAGC with validation
drawdown and shows that OAS maintains

2 Related Work

2.1 Retrieval-Augmented and
Tool-Augmented Language Agents

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) uses ex-
ternal knowledge to mitigate outdated knowledge,
factual hallucination, and weak evidence traceabil-
ity (Lewis et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2023). Early
RAG Systems typically retrieve once before gener-
ation; this is effective for knowledge-intensive QA
but limited by retrieval Noise and fixed workflows
in multi-hop reasoning. ReAct (Yao et al. 2023)
interleaves reasoning traces, actions, and observa-
Uons, moving retrieval from static preprocessing to
a tool action within the reasoning trajectory.
Search-augmented Feasoning systems let mod-
els decide When to search and how to form
queries. Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025) incorporates
Search into the RL environment, where model-
generated <search>.. -S/search> spans trigger
retrieval and returned evidence is appended as
<information>. --</information>. RAG-Gym
(Xiong et al., 2025) emphasizes process super-
vision and critic evaluation for agentic RAG,
while RLFactory (Chai et al., 2025) implements
a Benerate-parse-invoke-update loop with obser-
vation markers. These works define the setting
studied here: the model generates search actions,

receives observations, and continues reasoning be-
fore answering.

2.2 Reinforcement Learning for Language
Models and Tool-Use Rewards

Reinforcement learning is now central to language-
model post-training. RLHF (Ouyang et al., 2022)
PPO (Schulman et al., 2017), and GAE (Schutran
et al., 2016) provide foundations for instruction fol-
lowing and actor-critic training, while DeepSeek-
R1 (Guo et al., 2025) and DeepSeekMath (Shao
et al., 2024) show the role of outcome rewards
and GRPO-style methods in long-chain reasoning
Search-tool RL adds tool timing, query enhalae
tion, evidence use, and stopping decisions to this
setting.

Tool-use tasks therefore make reward design
and credit assignment harder. TooIRL (Qian et al
2025) argues that rewards should cover intermedi
ate decisions such as tool selection, execution, and
result use, not only final answer matching. Rea-
sonRAG (Zhang et al., 2025) decomposes agentic
RAG supervision into query generation, evidence
extraction, and answer generation, aiming to re-
duce outcome-only sparsity. Turn-level credit as-
signment work (Zeng et al., 2025) further shows
that sharing one trajectory-leve] advantage makes
different search turns difficult to attribute. ;

2.3. Training Instability in Multi-Turn Agent
Reinforcement Learning

Instability in LLM reinforcement-learning dynam-
ics is a recurring issue. Prior work reports entropy
collapse, reward variance collapse, policy stale-
ness, gradient spikes, catastrophic updates, and
advantage bias (Wang et al., 2025; Zheng et al.
2025; Dong et al., 2026a). RAGEN (Wang et al
2025) observes Echo Trap in multi-turn agent RL.
where local reward overfitting coincides with ve
ward variance cliffs, entropy drops, and gradient
spikes. More general LLM RL stability work links
token-level objectives to training-inference discrep-
ancy and policy staleness (Zheng et al., 2025).
Tool-use settings further amplify these issues.
Search-R i (Jin et al., 2025) and RLFactory (Chai
et al., 2025) feed external results back as observa-
tions and mask retrieved/tool-return tokens out of
the policy loss, marking tool feedback as different
from model-generated text. ARPO (Dong et al.
2026b) and AEPO (Dong et al., 2026a) show that
such feedback changes entropy, rollout sampling
and policy updates; SimpleTIR (Xue et al., 2025)
links performance collapse to feedback-induced
distributional drift and gradient norm explosion.

Understanding Tool-Integrated Reasoning (Lin and
Xu, 2025) further shows that reward shaping can
weaken main-task correctness signals under group-
normalized advantages. Together, these works
show that tool calls change the feedback distribu-
tion, advantage attribution, and gradient propaga-
tion on which model updates depend.

Overall, existing work shows that too! feedback
changes trajectory distributions, exploration, and
optimization signals, but less is known about how
observation tokens affect search-RL stability. Re-
trieved results both alter subsequent generation as
context and receive special training treatment, such
as exclusion from actor loss. They may still af-
fect value estimation, GAE, or advantage compu-
tation. This gap motivates our diagnostic focus
on VDD, ATE, AUS, OAGC, and token-domain

value/advantage gaps.
3 Trajectory-Level Instability Metrics

The failures in search-tool RL do not always mean
that the mode! fails to learn from the start. In PPO
training of Search-R1-style methods, we observe
a more subtle dynamic: the model first reaches a
useful validation score in the middle of training,
but later regresses, accompanied by degraded tool
use and abnormally long outputs. To distinguish
this phenomenon from jow-performing runs that
never reach useful validation performance, we for-
malize it as trajectory-tevel optimization instability.
We characterize it with four metrics: validation
drawdown (VDD), advantage tail expansion (ATE),
actor update stress (AUS), and observation-to-actor
GAE contamination (OAGC). Full symbol defini-

6 Experiments

This section evaluates whether observation-aware
stabilization (OAS) improves task performance,
training dynamics, and search-budget control. We
examine final QA performance across datasets, re-
trieval budgets, and model sizes; evaluate bounded
transfer to FEVER fact verification; analyze how
nVDD, ATE, AUS, and OAGC evolve together with

EM; and study retrieval behavior and search-budget
use during training.

6.1 Experimental Setup

We use a Search-R1-style search-tool RL frame-
work on three benchmark datasets: NQ, TriviaQA,
and HotpotQA. During each rollout, the model gen-
erates search actions, the retriever inserts observa-
tion tokens into the context, and the model con-
tinues reasoning before producing a final answer.
Main-text experiments use Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct
(Yang et al., 2024), with Qwen2.5-{.5B-Instruct
used as an additional scale check. We report fi-
nal EM across datasets and Top-k budgets with
k € {2.3,5}. We analyze nVDD, ATE, and OAGC
in the Qwen2.5-3B Top-3 ablations, and time-align
EM, nVDD, ATE, AUS, and OAGC for the con-
trolled Qwen2.5-1.5B NQ Top-3 PPO and OAS
trajectories. The OAS defaults are Qin = 0.2000,
B = 0.2812, Aops = 1.0000, and Asm = 0.0277;
all were frozen before formal evaluation. All meth-
ods within a setting use the same split, retrieval
budget, generation limits, and exact-match scorer:
full dataset, baseline, coefficient-selection, and sen-
sitivity details are in Appendix D.

7 Conclusion

This paper studies late-stage instability in search-
tool RL and identifies observation-token propaga-
tion through value learning and GAE as an under-
explored pathway. We introduce diagnostic met-
rics and OAS, a lightweight method combining ob-
servation residual decay, old-value anchoring, and
boundary smoothing. Across open-domain QA and
a bounded FEVER transfer, OAS improves final
task performance while reducing nVDD, ATE, and
OAGC. The time-aligned analysis connects increas-
ing ATE, AUS, and OAGC with validation draw-
down, while the retrieval-behavior analysis shows
lower late-stage search-budget saturation without
increased tool avoidance. The nearly unchanged
answer-string miss proxy does not establish im-
proved retrieval relevance or faithfulness. Together,
the diagnostics, mechanism analysis, and OAS in-
tervention characterize and mitigate instability in
search-tool RL.

Limitations

Our experiments evaluate Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B mod-
els across three open-domain QA datasets and fur-
ther extend to Qwen2.5-1,5B FEVER fact verifi-
cation under fixed Top-3 Wikipedia retrieval. The
FEVER results show that the stability and final-
performance benefits of OAS are not confined to
open-domain QA. We have not yet evaluated larger
model scales, real web-browsing environments,
multimodal tools, or more complex long-horizon
agent tasks, and leave validation in these settings
to future work.

Our mechanism analysis is not a complete causal
account of search-tool RL instability, OAGC,
domain-specific value-loss results, and the OAS
ablations are consistent with mask-induced actor-
critic domain mismatch, However, search-tool RL
instability may also depend on reward Sparsity, re-
triever noise, policy drift, long-sequence optimiza-
tion, and shifts in the sampling distribution, We
treat observation-side value and TD-residual prop-
agation as a measurable pathway targeted by OAS,
not as the only explanation for collapse.

Finally, OAS is designed primarily for PPO-style
training with a critic and GAE. Its components
may need to be reformulated for critic-free meth-
ods such as GRPO or systems with different state
representations, masking rules, and tool-feedback
formats. OAS also introduces additional hyperpa-
rameters and measurable training-time overhead,
Appendix D.2 reports one matched cost compar-
ison using Qwen2.5-1.5B on NQ with Top-3 re-
trieval, and Appendix D reports a one-at-a-time
coefficient sensitivity study in a Qwen2.5-3R NQ
Top-3 setting. Broader computational profiling
across model scales, hardware platforms, and task
regimes, broader coefficient Sweeps, and interac-
tions with other stabilization techniques remain
future work.

Potential risks also remain. Stabilizing retrieval-
augmented RL may make search agents more re-
liable at using retrieved Content, but retrieved ey-
idence can still be noisy, biased, outdated, or ma-
nipulated. More stable training therefore does not
remove the need for retrieval filtering, factuality
checks, and safety evaluation before deployment.
